newsitem.title: UK: Aviation insurers uncertain about liability change.
newsitem.headline: Aviation insurers uncertain about liability change.

text.p: The aviation insurance industry remains uncertain about how it will be affected by moves from the world's airlines to eliminate limits on passenger liability payouts.
For insurers it may mean higher claims, but it could also mean they might sell more liability cover, cut litigation costs, and allow them a chance to reverse the pressure on rates.

The aviation insurance market was not surprised by the International Air Transport Association's (IATA) announcement on Monday that a group of European airlines including KLM, SAS, and Swissair will not invoke the liability limits laid down in the Warsaw Convention when settling compensation claims resulting from death or injury.

It is expected to be the first in a series of similar announcements from other airlines stemming from last week's decision by the U.S. Department of Transport to drop its objections to an IATA proposal ending the limits.

Aviation insurers regarded the Warsaw limits - which meant airlines were obliged to settle at a maximum of $150,000 in Europe, $75,000 in the U.S. - as outdated and difficult to justify. In addition, insurers incurred high legal costs because they were obliged defend them against lawyers, particularly in the U.S., who found ways of getting round them.
Often the existence of the limits led to long and costly court cases in situations where an acceptable settlement could have been found much sooner.

Another problem was so-called 'forum shopping'. As claimants were able to try to take action either in the country the passenger was flying to, or where he bought the ticket, or in the airline's home country, they would often seek to pursue the case in whichever country offered the best chance of a payout or with the highest payment structure.

The new agreement does not, as some newspapers have reported, mean unlimited liability for airlines. Liability will be limited to the amount that the claimant can prove he has suffered as damages and is recoverable under applicable law in the country passenger's domicile country. In addition, the claimant would not have to prove negligence.

However the insurance industry is pretty certain that the outcome in many cases will be an increase the cost of claims. This leaves them with two issues. Firstly they have to ensure they benefit from selling more liability cover in the first place. The signs from current renewal season are that this has begun to happen, and that airlines are buying higher levels of liability cover.

But the more crucial issue is the price insurers sell it at. Aviation insurance rates have been pushed down because there are so many competitors struggling for the same business. While liability rates have not fallen as steeply as airliner hull rates, the market is still described as 'soft' - meaning underwriters are having to charge less than they would like to.

Airlines typically buy up to $200 million liability cover for any one hull, and $1 billion for any one loss. Couple this with a worldwide premium income of less than $2 billion, and the imbalance is clear.

The head of a major aviation insurer said: "The market's leading underwriters should assume the responsibility of re-rating each risk individually and charging as appropriate an additional premium which increased exposure deserves.
"Given the current soft state of the market, this requires a degree of fortitude, as it is all too tempting to become distracted by the problems excess capacity poses," he said.

Given the recent spate of air accidents, insurers will want to make sure they earn enough to stoke up their reserves. To this end they will argue the liability change is a reason to push up rates. If they are successful the airlines, themselves operating in a fiercely competitive market, would have to decide whether to pass the price rise onto the customer. But given the current state of the aviation insurance market, pushing through price rises may be an uphill struggle.
